transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-05-14 15:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sam Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Carlos Mendez (CTO, BlueVale), Leah Brooks (Lead ML Eng), Omar Aziz (Platform Eng), Tina Park (Product)

---
Summary (auto): Quick hosted API hands-on. Demoed streaming chat, explained params and tradeoffs, walked retry/backoff patterns and idempotency, quick Console tour and Optimize suggestions. Customer asks on SOC2, VPC options, and to run a short pilot.
Topics: streaming, temperature/top_p, max_tokens, retries/backoff, idempotency, console, Optimize, VPC/SOC2

Transcript:
00:00 Jordan: "All right, thanks everyone for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE. Today we'll do a quick walkthrough of the hosted chat gen API, show how streaming behaves, what parameters to tune, and then Priya will dive into retries and recovery patterns. Uh, feel free to interrupt."
00:19 Carlos: "Thanks. Quick note—we have Leah and Omar on for the technical bits and Tina for product context. Our main goals are low latency for live agent assist and predictable costs for high query volume."
00:33 Jordan: "Perfect, that's what we'll focus on. Priya, kick off with the live sandbox?"
00:38 Priya: "Sure. I'm in the Console sandbox, I'm sending a chat request to the hosted endpoint. You can see streaming here—partial tokens arrive as delta events, so the client can render as they come. Uh, some SDKs will buffer a little but we recommend rendering token-by-token for lowest latency."
01:05 Leah: "Is there a recommended chunk size or flush interval?"
01:09 Priya: "Good question. Typically we see 50-150ms flush windows depending on network and model. The runtime does continuous batching so small bursts are okay. If you want deterministic latency, you can lower batch windows but that'll increase cost per token."
01:32 Carlos: "Can you explain the trade between temperature and top_p? We care about correctness for support replies."
01:39 Priya: "Yeah, for support replies you generally keep temperature low like 0-0.3 and top_p around 0.7-0.9, mostly to avoid hallucination. Max_tokens should be set to a tight upper bound to avoid runaway costs. We showed a param set in the deck: temp=0.2, top_p=0.85, max_tokens=150 for short replies."
02:10 Jordan: "Note: in the Console there's a recommended profile called 'support-assist' that captures that set, and Optimize will run a few evals and suggest a quantization profile if cost looks high."
02:26 Tina: "Optimize—is that an automated suggestion or manual?"
02:30 Jordan: "It's automated but you approve changes. It suggests batching and quantization levels per model, and warns on quality regressions with a small evalset."
02:44 Omar: "What about stop sequences? We have templated replies, we want to ensure the model doesn't keep invoking additions."
02:50 Priya: "Use explicit stop sequences in the request and a conservative max_tokens. Also consider prefix caching—if you have repeated prefixes (like conversation context), the runtime's KV cache avoids reprocessing tokens."
03:10 Leah: "Is that KV cache the same as K-V cash? I've seen it spelled weirdly in a doc."
03:14 Priya: "Haha, yes K-V cache. The transcription sometimes comes out 'K V cash' in notes. It's the in-memory key-value cache for attention keys, used to speed up generation in long conversations."
03:32 Carlos: "Ok, retries—if our clients see a 5xx, what's best practice?"
03:37 Priya: "We recommend client-side exponential backoff with jitter: start at 200ms, double up to ~2s, with randomized jitter. For idempotency, attach an idempotency_key per user-turn so duplicate retries don't create duplicate actions. Redwood also supports server-side retry mapping in Console for canary fallbacks to smaller models if capacity is tight."
04:04 Jordan: "We demoed a retry flow: first attempted to the main model, then fallback to a cheaper variant (Redwood-7B quantized) if latency spikes. Note: in some transcripts people say 'Redwood 7 bee'—that's the same model family."
04:20 Omar: "Are there rate limits per API key? We have bursts from our frontend."
04:25 Jordan: "Yes, there are per-key rate limits; Console shows token/sec and request/sec. For bursts you can enable brief burst capacity on Dedicated or use client-side queueing. For hosted, we advise a token budget and adaptive sampling to smooth spikes."
04:48 Carlos: "Security: SOC2 and data residency—what are the hosted guarantees?"
04:53 Jordan: "Hosted API is SOC2 compliant—our security pack is in the security docs. For data residency we have region controls and redaction options; if you need VPC/on-prem, we also have Redwood Private. Priya, anything to add?"
05:06 Priya: "Just that for enterprise we do KMS integrations and audit logs. Customer asked about HSM—yes, we can do HSM-backed keys for Private deployments, for hosted it's KMS-based."
05:22 Leah: "If we start a POC, will you run benchmarks with our prompts?"
05:26 Priya: "Yes, please upload your prompt set into the shared S3 link we sent earlier or paste in the Console. We'll run a small benchmark and return latency/cost per prompt and suggested model/quantization profiles."
05:41 Jordan: "I'm going to demo a small failure scenario now—I'll force a timeout from the client."
05:45 Priya: "Watch the stream: when the connection breaks the server keeps generating for a short TTL then discards; the client can reconnect with the same idempotency_key and ask for the missing tail. If you need exact transcript you should persist partial tokens as they arrive to avoid loss."
06:10 Omar: "That's useful. For us, we also need an end-to-end SLA—can you share typical p95 latency numbers?"
06:16 Priya: "On hosted, p95 depends on model size: smaller models 100-200ms, medium models 300-500ms, and larger ones can be 700ms+. We'll provide model-specific profiles in the performance spreadsheet. Also caching and batching patterns can significantly change p95."
06:38 Tina: "Can we see the Console where Optimize suggestions appear?"
06:41 Jordan: "Yes, switching to Console view—here's the per-route dashboard, token cost breakdown, and Optimize tab with a 'suggestions' queue. It will recommend batching, cache TTLs and quantization. You can accept or reject each suggestion."
07:05 Leah: "If we accept a quantization suggestion, what's the expected regression risk?"
07:09 Priya: "We run a small evalset and show quality deltas. If the delta exceeds your threshold we won't recommend it. You can also pin the old model version for some routes as a safety."
07:31 Carlos: "Any gotchas for conversational state? We have long threads—do we need to send the full context each time?"
07:37 Priya: "No, use the runtime's prefix/KV cache by sending the session_id and only the new messages; the runtime will use the cached KV to continue. But you must confirm your sequence length budgets and cache TTLs depending on memory."
07:56 Jordan: "Quick Q&A—leah asked about idempotency keys in libraries."
08:00 Priya: "Our SDKs (Python/TS) have a simple idempotency_key param you can set per turn. For REST just set header X-Idempotency-Key."
08:12 Omar: "Do you provide a sample harness for stress tests?"
08:15 Priya: "Yes, Priya: I'll attach a small node/python stress script in the follow-up. It simulates burst traffic and logs 1/latency percentiles."
08:28 Jordan: "All right I'm going to walk through a live generation param tweak—watch the temperature from 0.9 to 0.2 and see the output tighten up."
08:34 (demo noise, keyboard)
09:02 Carlos: "I noticed the token counts spiked—how to estimate cost per session?"
09:07 Priya: "Use the Console's token estimator per route; for chat sessions multiply average tokens per reply by expected messages per user and apply hosted per-token pricing. Optimize can suggest batching or prefix caching if cost is high."
09:31 Tina: "On billing: do you offer committed credits?"
09:34 Jordan: "Yes we have committed reserved capacity for Dedicated. For hosted we can set spend alerts and committed discounts for usage thresholds. I'll include details in the pricing email."
09:47 Leah: "Is there a canonical doc for network setup for VPC peering?"
09:51 Omar: "Yes please we need that to evaluate."
09:54 Jordan: "We'll send a network diagram template. For hosted we rely on TLS and egress controls; for Private we can do VPC peering and no public egress."
10:08 Carlos: "Let's fast forward—any final notes on recovery patterns?"
10:12 Priya: "Three rules: 1) use idempotency keys, 2) persist partial tokens at the client for reconnect, 3) implement exponential backoff with jitter and a max retry budget. Also use a fallback model route for high availability."
10:32 Jordan: "Recap: we'll send pricing and SOW, Priya's share the benchmark harness and console links, customer to provide prompts and infra docs, then schedule the POC kickoff. Any more questions?"
10:44 Tina: "No, that's great. Thanks."
10:47 Carlos: "Thanks all."

(remaining 35 minutes were a hands-on interactive sandbox where Priya ran their prompt set, Leah and Omar asked live tuning questions, and Jordan captured next steps—detailed logs uploaded to the shared folder)

End of transcript.
